chapter: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington
title: Whether Ellington meant it and how the band had changed
summary: Barnet thinks Duke believed it, noting his age and the changed band after Hodges and Strayhorn.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Yeah, but he went further -- besides that, he said that if you get emotional about your music then you lose control of it and you have to have control of it in order to evoke emotion in the listener. And if you're involved in your emotions then you're not in control and you're not going to be concerned with the effect of the music on the listener.
Well, I think he's probably right in that context.

If you get overly exuberant in your playing, you get excited, you have a tendency to maybe over-estimate your ability and attempt things that you wouldn't normally attempt. On the other hand, I mean, some wonderful things have happened out of things like that.
But you're saying overly emotional but Duke said no emotion.
He said no emotion. No, I don't agree with that.

But do you think he really meant it, because you said that you felt that emotion could very often be a wonderful inspiration, and Duke said absolutely not. Do you think that he was just arguing, taking a different point of view, or do you think he really believed that? I found it hard to believe that he really believed it.

I thought he believed that, and I had reasons for it, for believing that he did believe it. Now, I'm not saying this derogatorily or anything, but don't forget, we were looking at a man in his 70s at that time.

A lot of things about Duke had changed. The band had changed considerably. And I think that his thinking about the band, the very thing, the kind of things the band was playing, along those times -- along about that time, were -- well, some of them, so far as I'm concerned, didn't make it. I felt cheated. Now, this could have been by the fact that, you know, maybe Johnny's gone and Strayhorn was gone, and the trumpet section was kind of in an uproar back there. And Duke was more or less getting in his ivory tower. I mean he'd sit up in the room there, all by himself, and I had a feeling that he was withdrawn a little bit, from the Duke that I had known, you know, in previous years. However,
who's going to fault that? Everybody gets old.

And I guess as you get older you become very firmly fixed with ideas. I find myself becoming very dogmatic about certain things now that maybe before I would be hanging on a cliff, yes I will, no I won't, and now I have pretty definite opinions about a lot of things that I didn't have before. So I think that had a lot to do with it. That's what I had attributed it to. I've told this a lot -- of course when anybody says we got into an argument, no.
I don't mean a hostile argument, but I mean a spirited argument.
A spirited discussion. You were taking two different points of view very strongly.
